learning_objective: 🎯 Become a reporter! Learn to write factual, objective, and past-tense accounts of events, accidents, or school functions.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: A report is a factual description of an event or an incident that has ALREADY taken place. It is strictly informative, without any personal opinions or emotions.
Used for school magazines (e.g., Annual Day, Sports Meet). Format: Heading, By-line. Body includes what, when, where, chief guest, highlights of the event, and conclusion.
Written for the public. Format: Headline, By-line, followed by 'Place, Date:' at the start of the first paragraph. Focuses on damage, rescue operations, police action, and quotes from eyewitnesses.
Since the event is over, reports are always written in the Past Tense. Use Passive Voice to sound objective (e.g., 'The injured were taken to the hospital' instead of 'People took the injured...').
The very first paragraph (lead paragraph) must answer the crucial 5 Ws: What happened? Where did it happen? When did it happen? Who was involved? Why/How did it happen?

fun_activity.title: 🎤 The 30-Second Reporter
fun_activity.instructions: Imagine a dog stole a student's lunchbox in the playground. Report it in one passive-voice sentence. (Example: 'A student's lunchbox was snatched by a stray dog near the swings at 12 PM.')

exam_tips: 📌 NEVER use first-person pronouns (I, me, my, we) in a report. You are an observer.
📌 For newspaper reports, don't forget to write the Place and Date (e.g., New Delhi, 15 Oct:) before starting the body.
📌 Keep the headline short, punchy, and grammatically incomplete (e.g., '10 Injured in Bus Mishap').
quick_recap: ⭐ Reports are factual; Articles are opinionated.
⭐ Always use Simple Past and Past Perfect tenses.
⭐ The logical flow: Intro (5 Ws) -> Details of event -> Conclusion/Action taken.
